concepts.name: Linear equation
concepts.statement: A linear equation in the unknowns x₁, x₂, …, xₙ may be written in the form a₁x₁ + a₂x₂ + … + aₙxₙ = b, where a₁, a₂, …, aₙ are real numbers known as coefficients; we also say that x₁, x₂, …, xₙ are the variables in the equation. Each term on the left is the product of a constant and the first power of an unknown, so the equation of any line can be expressed in the form ax + by = c, vertical lines such as x = 3 included.

forms.condition: the equation of a line, two unknowns

concepts.name: System of linear equations
concepts.statement: By a system of linear equations, or a linear system, we mean a set of linear equations written in a common set of unknowns.

concepts.name: Solution of a linear system
concepts.statement: A solution to a linear system is simply a set of numbers x₁ = s₁, x₂ = s₂, …, xₙ = sₙ that satisfy all the equations in the system; to check that (x, y) = (2, 3) is a solution of a system, we verify that each of its equations is true at those values.

concepts.name: Solution space
concepts.statement: We call the set of all solutions the solution space of the linear system. For equations in two unknowns it is seen graphically as the points where the lines of the equations meet; in three unknowns, where the planes meet.

concepts.name: Solutions to sets of linear equations
concepts.statement: Given a set of linear equations, there are either infinitely many points, exactly one point, or no points that satisfy every equation in the set. This is a general principle to which we will frequently return.

concepts.name: Solution sets as lines and planes
concepts.statement: The solutions to a linear equation in two unknowns form a straight line, and the solutions to a linear equation in three unknowns form a plane, such as y = 0 in the plane and z = 0 in space. The solution space of a set of equations is the intersection of these lines or planes: two planes typically meet in a line and three planes in a point, though in special cases two planes are parallel or three planes have no common point.

concepts.name: More equations, fewer solutions
concepts.statement: A single equation has infinitely many solutions; as we add equations, we add conditions, which lead to a smaller number of solutions, and eventually there are too many equations and no point satisfies all of them. So we come to expect that more equations than unknowns give no solutions and fewer equations than unknowns give infinitely many, though there are exceptions: two equations in two unknowns may be parallel lines with no solution, and three equations in two unknowns may have a single solution.

concepts.name: Recognizing a linear equation
concepts.statement: Deciding whether an equation is linear: it is linear when it can be rewritten with each term the product of a constant and the first power of an unknown, as x = 3z − 4y can be written x + 4y − 3z = 0, and it is not linear when a term such as xy or y² appears.

concepts.name: Checking a solution of a linear system
concepts.statement: Checking whether a set of values is a solution of a linear system by substituting it into every equation and verifying that each equation is true; a set of values that fails even one equation is not a solution, and finding more than one solution suggests there are infinitely many.

concepts.name: Gaussian elimination
concepts.statement: Gaussian elimination is our primary tool for describing the solution space of a linear system. Using replacement and scaling operations we eliminate the first variable from all but one equation and proceed to the next variables working left to right until the system is triangular, then use back substitution moving right to left until it is decoupled. On the augmented matrix, the same scaling, interchange, and replacement operations construct the one reduced row echelon matrix that is row equivalent to it, and the process of constructing this matrix is called Gaussian elimination.

concepts.name: Decoupled system
concepts.statement: A linear system in which each equation has only one variable, so that it prescribes a specific value for that variable, is called decoupled; such a system has exactly one solution, which can be read off the equations.

concepts.name: Triangular system
concepts.statement: A system such as x + 2y − 2z = −4, −y + z = 3, 3z = 3 is called a triangular system due to the shape formed by its coefficients: each equation involves fewer of the leading variables than the one above it.

concepts.name: Back substitution
concepts.statement: Triangular systems are easily solved by back substitution: the last equation gives the value of the last variable, which is substituted into the equations above it to obtain a new system having the same solutions; repeating this moves through the variables right to left and arrives at a decoupled system, which shows there is exactly one solution.

concepts.name: Scaling, interchange, and replacement
concepts.statement: Three operations transform a system of linear equations into a new system of equations having the same solution space. Scaling: we can multiply one equation by a nonzero number. Interchange: interchanging equations will not change the set of solutions. Replacement: we may multiply one equation by a real number and add it to another equation. Each can be reversed, which is why the solution space is the same; on an augmented matrix they act on the rows.

concepts.name: Matrix
concepts.statement: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers, such as the array that records the numerical data of a linear system once we forget about the variables; its rows are what scaling, interchange, and replacement act on, and a matrix with three rows and five columns is a 3 × 5 matrix.

concepts.name: Augmented matrix
concepts.statement: When writing a linear system, we always write the variables in the same order in each equation; we then construct an augmented matrix by simply forgetting about the variables and recording the numerical data in a rectangular array. The vertical line reminds us where the equals signs appear in the equations, and the entries to its left are the coefficients of the equations.

concepts.name: Coefficient matrix
concepts.statement: We sometimes choose to focus only on the coefficients of the system, in which case we write the coefficient matrix: the entries of the augmented matrix to the left of the vertical line, without the column of constants.

concepts.name: Row equivalence
concepts.statement: The symbol ∼ between two matrices indicates that they are related by a sequence of scaling, interchange, and replacement operations; since these operations act on the rows of the matrices, we say the matrices are row equivalent. The linear systems corresponding to two row equivalent augmented matrices have the same solution space.

concepts.name: Leading entry
concepts.statement: If we move across a row of a matrix from left to right, the first nonzero entry we encounter is the leading entry in the row.

concepts.name: Reduced row echelon form
concepts.statement: A matrix is in reduced row echelon form if: when the entries in a row are all zero, the same is true of any row below it; the first nonzero entry in each row, its leading entry, is 1; the leading entry in any row is to the right of the leading entries in all the rows above it; and a leading entry is the only nonzero entry in its column. We call a matrix in reduced row echelon form a reduced row echelon matrix, whether it is an augmented matrix or a coefficient matrix.

concepts.name: Uniqueness of the reduced row echelon form
concepts.statement: For any given matrix, there is exactly one reduced row echelon matrix to which it is row equivalent. There is a sequence of row operations that transforms any matrix into one in reduced row echelon form, and the conditions that define reduced row echelon matrices guarantee that this matrix is unique.

concepts.name: Free variable
concepts.statement: When the equations of a reduced row echelon matrix place no restriction on the value of a variable, so that we obtain a solution for any value of it, we call it a free variable; the presence of a free variable means the linear system has infinitely many solutions.

concepts.name: Basic variable
concepts.statement: The variables that are determined once we make a choice of the free variables are called basic variables.

concepts.name: Parametric description
concepts.statement: A description of the solution space in which the basic variables are written in terms of the free variables, such as x = −1 − 2z, y = 2 − z, is called a parametric description of the solution space.

concepts.name: Reading the solution space from a reduced row echelon matrix
concepts.statement: Describing the solution space from the reduced row echelon form of an augmented matrix: write the linear system it corresponds to; an equation 0 = 0 imposes no restriction and is ignored; an equation 0 = 1 is not true for any values, so there is no solution; otherwise write the basic variables in terms of the free variables, which gives a unique solution when there is no free variable and infinitely many when there is one.

concepts.name: Computing in Sage
concepts.statement: Sage uses the standard operators +, -, *, / and ^ for the usual arithmetic operations. Commands on separate lines are evaluated in turn and only the result of the last is displayed unless print is used; the result of one command may be given a name and referred to in a later command. Sage is written in Python, and Python code may be entered into a Sage cell.

concepts.name: Entering a matrix in Sage
concepts.statement: A matrix is created in Sage by matrix(m, n, [entries]), whose three arguments are the number of rows, the number of columns, and the entries listed by row inside square brackets, separated by commas; or by listing its rows, matrix([[…], […]]). There is no way of specifying whether a matrix is augmented or a coefficient matrix, so it is up to us to interpret the results.

concepts.name: Finding a reduced row echelon matrix in Sage
concepts.statement: Giving a matrix a name, A = matrix(…), its reduced row echelon form is found by A.rref(). If all the entries are integers, Sage computes with rational numbers, and A.rref().numerical_approx(digits=4) shows a decimal approximation. From the reduced row echelon form of an augmented matrix we describe the solution space of the linear system.

concepts.name: Rows and columns of a matrix
concepts.statement: A matrix has a certain number of rows and columns: a matrix with three rows and five columns is a 3 × 5 matrix, and a matrix with the same number of rows as columns, n, is an n × n matrix.

concepts.name: Augmentation of a matrix
concepts.statement: We say that a matrix B is an augmentation of a matrix A when it is obtained from A by adding some more columns; an augmented matrix is an augmentation of its coefficient matrix.

concepts.name: Augmentation Principle
concepts.statement: If matrix B is an augmentation of matrix A, then the reduced row echelon form of B is an augmentation of the reduced row echelon form of A. In particular, the reduced row echelon form of a coefficient matrix is found by looking inside the reduced row echelon form of the augmented matrix.

concepts.name: Computational effort of row reduction
concepts.statement: Measuring effort by the number of multiplications and additions, scaling a row of an n × n matrix requires n operations, an interchange none, and a replacement 2n. Roughly n² replacements and n scalings are needed to reach the reduced row echelon form, about 2n³ + n² operations in all, so the number of operations required to find the reduced row echelon form of an n × n matrix is roughly proportional to n³; a more careful accounting gives ⅔n³. If the size of the matrix grows by a factor of 10, the effort grows by a factor of 1000; a trillion equations in a trillion unknowns would take about 10¹⁶ years at a trillion operations a second.

concepts.name: Pivot position
concepts.statement: A pivot position in a matrix A is the position of a leading entry in the reduced row echelon matrix of A. We refer to pivot positions by their row and column number, saying, for instance, that there is a pivot position in the third row and fourth column.

concepts.name: Pivots per row and column
concepts.statement: A row contains at most one pivot position and a column contains at most one, so a 3 × 5 matrix has at most three pivot positions and so does a 5 × 3 matrix. A matrix with a pivot position in every row and every column must necessarily have the same number of rows and columns.

concepts.name: Two Fundamental Questions
concepts.statement: When we encounter a linear system, we often ask two questions. Existence: is there a solution to the linear system? Uniqueness: if the linear system is consistent, is the solution unique or are there infinitely many solutions? These two questions represent two sides of a coin that appear in many variations throughout our explorations; the location of the pivots influences the answers to both.

concepts.name: Consistent system
concepts.statement: If there is a solution to a linear system, we say that the system is consistent.

concepts.name: Inconsistent system
concepts.statement: If there is no solution to a linear system, we say it is inconsistent.

concepts.name: Inconsistency and a pivot in the rightmost column
concepts.statement: A linear system is inconsistent if and only if there is a pivot position in the rightmost column of the corresponding augmented matrix. Such a row says 0x + 0y + 0z = 1, which cannot be satisfied for any (x, y, z), while a row whose entries are all zero says 0 = 0 and has no effect on the solution space.

concepts.name: A pivot in every row gives a consistent system
concepts.statement: If every row of the coefficient matrix has a pivot position, then the corresponding system of linear equations is consistent: by the Augmentation Principle the reduced row echelon form of the coefficient matrix sits inside that of the augmented matrix, so there is no way to obtain a pivot in the rightmost column of the augmented matrix.

concepts.name: Pivots and the uniqueness of solutions
concepts.statement: Suppose that we consider a consistent linear system. If every column of the coefficient matrix contains a pivot position, then the system has a unique solution. If there is a column in the coefficient matrix that contains no pivot position, then the system has infinitely many solutions. Columns that contain a pivot position correspond to basic variables while columns that do not correspond to free variables; we adopt the convention that free variables correspond to columns without a pivot position.

concepts.name: Equations needed for a unique solution
concepts.statement: When a linear system has a unique solution, every column of the coefficient matrix has a pivot position; since every row contains at most one pivot position, there must be at least as many rows as columns, so the linear system has at least as many equations as variables. A consistent system with more variables than equations must have a free variable and so infinitely many solutions.

concepts.name: Reading existence and uniqueness from the pivots
concepts.statement: Determining whether a linear system is consistent, and whether its solution is unique, from the pivot positions of its reduced row echelon augmented matrix: a pivot in the rightmost column means the system is inconsistent; otherwise a pivot in every column of the coefficient matrix means a unique solution and a column without one means infinitely many, the pivot columns naming the basic variables and the others the free variables, from which a parametric description is written.
